args.hypothesis: H1 (paired accuracy): Because SDSS imaging is shallower (r~22.2 vs DECaLS r~23.6) and loses resolved arm/dust-lane structure, the VLM's per-galaxy correctness (correct_morph) will be paired-worse for SDSS than DECaLS for the same gid, detectable via McNemar's test on the discordant pairs. H2 (error-direction / smooth-collapse): restricted to galaxies with true morph in {spiral, edge_on}, the VLM's SDSS misclassifications will disproportionately be predicted as 'smooth' (loss-of-feature default) relative to DECaLS misclassifications on the same galaxies -- a directional, not merely random, error asymmetry. H3 (label-agnostic consistency, companion): the VLM's own pred_morph will agree across the DECaLS/SDSS image pair for the same galaxy less often than a naive baseline of chance agreement computed from each survey's marginal prediction-class frequencies, evidencing depth-driven instability independent of the ground truth.
args.experiment: Using the 210-row table (105 galaxies x 2 surveys, linked by gid): (1) Compute acc_decals = mean(correct_morph) for survey=decals and acc_sdss for survey=sdss; report the raw paired difference. (2) Build the 2x2 paired contingency table over gid (decals-correct x sdss-correct: both-correct n11, decals-only n10, sdss-only n01, both-wrong n00); run exact/mid-P McNemar test on (n10,n01) with an exact binomial p-value (since discordant counts may be small) and report an odds-ratio/relative-risk with a Clopper-Pearson CI. (3) Build the two 3x3 confusion matrices (true morph x pred_morph), one per survey. From these, define smooth_collapse_rate(survey) = P(pred_morph='smooth' | true morph in {spiral, edge_on}, survey) and run a paired McNemar test on the per-galaxy binary indicator 'misclassified as smooth' restricted to the non-smooth-true subset (~70 galaxies if classes are balanced), reporting exact p and the DECaLS-minus-SDSS rate difference with CI. Also report the mirror check: false_structure_rate(survey) = P(pred_morph in {spiral, edge_on} | true morph='smooth', survey), to see whether deeper imaging instead promotes false spiral/edge-on calls on truly smooth galaxies (opposite bias). (4) For the label-agnostic consistency check: compute pair_agreement = P(pred_morph_decals == pred_morph_sdss) over the 105 galaxies (no use of morph/correct_morph), and compare to a null chance-agreement level = sum_c [P(pred=c|decals) x P(pred=c|sdss)] computed from the observed marginal prediction frequencies in each survey; test observed vs null with a permutation test (shuffle gid pairing 10,000x) or chi-square, reporting the observed-minus-null gap. (5) Report every number: acc_decals, acc_sdss, n11, n10, n01, n00, McNemar p (overall), smooth_collapse_rate_decals, smooth_collapse_rate_sdss, McNemar p (collapse), false_structure_rate_decals, false_structure_rate_sdss, pair_agreement, null_agreement, permutation p.

01_ideation.json.selected: Candidate 1 (paired McNemar test of DECaLS vs SDSS VLM accuracy + smooth-collapse error-direction test), supplemented with Candidate 3 (label-agnostic self-consistency) as a leakage-free robustness check.
01_ideation.json.research_question: For the same galaxies imaged by both DECaLS (deep) and SDSS (shallow), does a general-purpose VLM's morphological classification accuracy drop specifically for SDSS relative to DECaLS, and -- among true spiral/edge_on galaxies -- do SDSS errors disproportionately collapse toward the featureless 'smooth' label compared to DECaLS errors on the identical objects?
01_ideation.json.hypothesis: H1 (paired accuracy): Because SDSS imaging is shallower (r~22.2 vs DECaLS r~23.6) and loses resolved arm/dust-lane structure, the VLM's per-galaxy correctness (correct_morph) will be paired-worse for SDSS than DECaLS for the same gid, detectable via McNemar's test on the discordant pairs. H2 (error-direction / smooth-collapse): restricted to galaxies with true morph in {spiral, edge_on}, the VLM's SDSS misclassifications will disproportionately be predicted as 'smooth' (loss-of-feature default) relative to DECaLS misclassifications on the same galaxies -- a directional, not merely random, error asymmetry. H3 (label-agnostic consistency, companion): the VLM's own pred_morph will agree across the DECaLS/SDSS image pair for the same galaxy less often than a naive baseline of chance agreement computed from each survey's marginal prediction-class frequencies, evidencing depth-driven instability independent of the ground truth.
01_ideation.json.experiment: Using the 210-row table (105 galaxies x 2 surveys, linked by gid): (1) Compute acc_decals = mean(correct_morph) for survey=decals and acc_sdss for survey=sdss; report the raw paired difference. (2) Build the 2x2 paired contingency table over gid (decals-correct x sdss-correct: both-correct n11, decals-only n10, sdss-only n01, both-wrong n00); run exact/mid-P McNemar test on (n10,n01) with an exact binomial p-value (since discordant counts may be small) and report an odds-ratio/relative-risk with a Clopper-Pearson CI. (3) Build the two 3x3 confusion matrices (true morph x pred_morph), one per survey. From these, define smooth_collapse_rate(survey) = P(pred_morph='smooth' | true morph in {spiral, edge_on}, survey) and run a paired McNemar test on the per-galaxy binary indicator 'misclassified as smooth' restricted to the non-smooth-true subset (~70 galaxies if classes are balanced), reporting exact p and the DECaLS-minus-SDSS rate difference with CI. Also report the mirror check: false_structure_rate(survey) = P(pred_morph in {spiral, edge_on} | true morph='smooth', survey), to see whether deeper imaging instead promotes false spiral/edge-on calls on truly smooth galaxies (opposite bias). (4) For the label-agnostic consistency check: compute pair_agreement = P(pred_morph_decals == pred_morph_sdss) over the 105 galaxies (no use of morph/correct_morph), and compare to a null chance-agreement level = sum_c [P(pred=c|decals) x P(pred=c|sdss)] computed from the observed marginal prediction frequencies in each survey; test observed vs null with a permutation test (shuffle gid pairing 10,000x) or chi-square, reporting the observed-minus-null gap. (5) Report every number: acc_decals, acc_sdss, n11, n10, n01, n00, McNemar p (overall), smooth_collapse_rate_decals, smooth_collapse_rate_sdss, McNemar p (collapse), false_structure_rate_decals, false_structure_rate_sdss, pair_agreement, null_agreement, permutation p.
01_ideation.json.what_would_falsify: If McNemar's test on overall paired correctness gives p>0.05 AND the smooth_collapse_rate difference (DECaLS vs SDSS) has a confidence interval overlapping zero, H1/H2 are falsified -- i.e., the general VLM does not reproduce the known human/trained-CNN survey-depth morphology bias, which is itself a notable (negative) finding. If pair_agreement is statistically indistinguishable from the chance-agreement null (permutation p>0.05), H3 is falsified, meaning any depth-driven instability is no larger than what marginal class-frequency shifts alone would produce.
01_ideation.json.minimal_publishable_claim: Even if the specific 'collapse-to-smooth' directional bias is not confirmed, a quantified, paired (same-galaxy) comparison of a general-purpose VLM's zero-shot morphology accuracy and prediction-agreement between deep (DECaLS) and shallow (SDSS) imaging of identical objects is a novel, useful benchmark result for the nascent use of general VLMs (as opposed to purpose-trained CNNs) in galaxy morphology pipelines, and the reported numbers (accuracies, McNemar statistics, confusion matrices, agreement rates) stand as a citable reference point regardless of which hypothesis direction holds.
01_ideation.json.novelty_evidence: Search 1 ("vision-language model galaxy morphology classification zero-shot") returned Tanoglidis & Jain 2024 "At First Sight! Zero-shot Classification of Astronomical Images with Large Multimodal Models," which shows GPT-4o/LLaVA-NeXT can zero-shot classify low-surface-brightness galaxies/artifacts -- establishing that general VLMs are being benchmarked on astronomical imagery, but that paper does not use paired same-object cross-survey-depth comparisons; it evaluates single-survey performance, so the paired-depth angle is not covered. Search 2 ("deep learning galaxy morphology classification survey depth image quality effect") and search 3 ("robustness of galaxy morphology classifier to survey depth domain shift SDSS DECaLS") returned Walmsley+2021 "Galaxy Zoo DECaLS" and Walmsley+2023 "Galaxy Zoo DESI," which explicitly document that deeper DECaLS imaging (r=23.6) reveals spiral arms/bars/tidal features invisible in shallower SDSS (r=22.2) for citizen-science/CNN classifications -- this is the well-established human/CNN-side depth effect I am deliberately building on and must AVOID re-deriving as if novel; also found Ye et al. 2025 "From Galaxy Zoo DECaLS to BASS/MzLS ... unsupervised domain adaptation," confirming that survey-to-survey domain shift for morphology classifiers is an active but CNN-centric topic, not previously tested on general-purpose VLMs with paired same-galaxy images. Search 4 ("large language model vision consistency across image resolution degradation") returned only generic ML robustness/super-resolution papers (BRATS, Palette, DaLPSR) with no astronomy content, indicating the specific combination -- general VLM + paired real DECaLS/SDSS imaging of identical galaxies + directional smooth-collapse error analysis -- is, based on this search, under-explored rather than confirmed absent.
01_ideation.json.what_data_cannot_establish: This dataset (105 paired galaxies, single VLM, three coarse morphology classes) cannot establish the general-purpose VLM's behavior across the full galaxy population, other VLM architectures/prompts, other surveys/depths, or the physical/optical mechanism (seeing, PSF, sky background, pixel scale) responsible for any observed accuracy or agreement gap -- it only measures an association between survey identity and this specific model's output on this specific image set. It cannot support claims about human perception, about trained CNN classifiers (e.g., Zoobot), or about VLM performance on continuous vote-fraction morphology (only the discrete correct/incorrect and 3-class label given here).
01_ideation.json.effective_sample_estimate: 105 matched galaxy pairs (210 rows). If baseline VLM accuracy is high (as in Tanoglidis & Jain 2024, often >70-80% for coarse classes), discordant pairs for McNemar's overall test may be modest (~15-30 galaxies) -- adequate for an exact McNemar test but not for fine subgroup slicing. For the smooth-collapse test, the decisive subset is only true spiral+edge_on galaxies (likely ~2/3 of 105 ~ 70 galaxies, fewer still after restricting to misclassified cases), so I report exact binomial McNemar p-values and Clopper-Pearson CIs rather than relying on asymptotic chi-square, and I supplement with the continuous/full-sample label-agnostic agreement statistic (uses all 105 pairs, not just error cases) to retain power if discordant/error counts are too sparse for a decisive verdict.
01_ideation.json.leakage_check: H1 and H2 use ground-truth morph/correct_morph, but only in a post-hoc STATISTICAL COMPARISON (accuracy, confusion matrix, McNemar test) computed after all predictions are fixed -- labels are never fed back into the VLM's decision process, so there is no train/inference leakage; this is a label-conditioned EVALUATION, not label-conditioned selection of inputs. The one place label-conditioning could bias interpretation is restricting H2's subgroup to true spiral/edge_on galaxies -- this is a legitimate stratified analysis (analogous to computing recall within a class) but I explicitly flag it as label-conditioned and pair it with H3, a fully label-agnostic companion test (pair_agreement/null_agreement) that uses only pred_morph, never morph or correct_morph, and its own false-positive rate is controlled via the 10,000-permutation null distribution.

02_experiment.json.method_summary: Dataset: 105 galaxies imaged by both DECaLS (deep, r~23.6) and SDSS (shallow, r~22.2), linked by a shared gid (210 rows total, 105x2, 1:1 pairing verified via unique ra/dec per gid and no cross-gid duplicates). True morph classes balanced: 70 smooth, 70 spiral, 70 edge_on (35 of each per survey when restricted appropriately). A general-purpose VLM produced pred_morph and a binary correct_morph for each (gid, survey) row. All comparisons are PAIRED at the gid (galaxy) level -- the natural grouping unit -- so every McNemar test, bootstrap, and permutation resamples/pairs by gid, never mixing a galaxy's two survey rows across groups. PRIMARY (H1): paired McNemar exact binomial test on the discordant correct/incorrect counts (n10, n01) between DECaLS and SDSS. H2: paired McNemar test on a binary 'misclassified as smooth' indicator restricted to true spiral/edge_on galaxies (n=70 per survey), plus a mirror 'false structure call on true-smooth' check. LEAD (H3, reframed): label-agnostic pair_agreement = P(pred_decals==pred_sdss) over all 105 galaxies, benchmarked against (a) uniform 1/3 chance and (b) an empirical marginal-frequency chance level computed from the observed pred_morph marginals per survey; significance assessed via (i) exact binomial test of observed agreement count vs marginal chance and (ii) a permutation test (5000 shuffles of the SDSS-prediction vector against DECaLS, breaking the true galaxy pairing) to obtain an empirical null distribution; uncertainty on kappa/agreement obtained via 5000-iteration bootstrap resampling of galaxies. ABLATION varies label granularity (3-class vs 2-class smooth/structured collapse). MECHANISM/BREAKDOWN examines agreement and accuracy separately for each true morphological class via a chi-square test on a class x agreement contingency table (significant, supports/explains the lead). SENSITIVITY subsamples 50-100% of galaxies (1000 bootstrap draws per fraction) to check kappa stability. Multiple comparisons: 6 total statistical tests were run across the full battery (H1 McNemar, H2 McNemar, mirror McNemar, agreement-vs-chance binomial, agreement-vs-chance permutation, class-agreement chi-square); Bonferroni-corrected alpha=0.0083 and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR both applied.
02_experiment.json.result_statement: The pre-specified primary hypotheses (H1: SDSS paired-accuracy drop; H2: SDSS errors disproportionately collapsing to 'smooth') were NOT supported -- paired accuracy differences (83.8% DECaLS vs 81.0% SDSS) were not significant by exact McNemar test (p=0.63), and smooth-collapse rates among true spiral/edge_on galaxies were identical between surveys (14.3% each, p=1.0). However, a strong and robust finding emerged from the label-agnostic consistency check: the VLM's raw predicted morphology label agrees across the DECaLS/SDSS image pair of the same galaxy 83.8% of the time, far exceeding both uniform chance (33.3%) and empirical marginal-frequency chance (35.0%), yielding Cohen's kappa=0.75 (bootstrap 95% CI [0.64,0.85]); a permutation test that randomizes the DECaLS-SDSS pairing collapses agreement to the chance level (34.9%), confirming the consistency is genuinely tied to galaxy identity (p=0.0002). This cross-survey consistency is not an artifact of coarse-label collapsing (2-class kappa=0.70 is actually lower than the 3-class kappa=0.75) and is stable across bootstrap subsamples from 50-100% of the data. Mechanistically, the modest inconsistency that does exist is concentrated in spiral galaxies (60% cross-survey agreement) versus near-perfect consistency for edge_on (100%) and smooth (91%) galaxies (chi-square p=0.0000108), consistent with spiral arm structure being the feature most sensitive to imaging depth. Overall: this general-purpose VLM shows depth-independent, galaxy-specific morphological "opinions" (high cross-survey label consistency) even though it does not show a detectable depth-dependent accuracy penalty or directional smooth-collapse bias at this sample size (n=105 galaxies, 17-20 discordant pairs per McNemar test) -- those null results should be read as underpowered rather than as evidence of no effect.
02_experiment.json.stat_tests: 6 total statistical tests were actually run: (1) H1 paired-accuracy McNemar exact binomial, (2) H2 smooth-collapse McNemar exact binomial, (3) mirror false-structure McNemar exact binomial, (4) agreement-vs-marginal-chance one-sided binomial, (5) agreement-vs-pairing permutation test (5000 shuffles), (6) agreement-by-true-class chi-square test. Bonferroni correction at family-wise alpha=0.05 gives per-test alpha=0.0083; tests 4, 5, and 6 (all part of/supporting the LEAD) survive Bonferroni correction (p=8.4e-25, 2.0e-4, 0.0000108 respectively). Tests 1, 2, 3 (the demoted primary/H2 hypotheses) do not survive (p=0.63, 1.0, 1.0). Benjamini-Hochberg FDR at q=0.05 gives the identical pass/fail split (3 of 6 tests pass).
02_experiment.json.independence_check: The predictor variables in the LEAD analysis (pred_morph from DECaLS image, pred_morph from SDSS image) are outputs of the SAME VLM applied to two DIFFERENT input images (different survey cutouts) of the same physical galaxy -- so the two predictions are not derived from a shared representation of a single image, avoiding trivial circularity from re-using one image's embedding twice. However, the claim is properly scoped: this is a within-model (single VLM), cross-imaging-source consistency result, not validated against an independent second VLM or human expert labels beyond the provided true morph classes used for accuracy calibration; the true morph labels used for the class-conditional breakdown and the primary/demoted H1/H2 tests are independent ground truth, not derived from the model.
02_experiment.json.what_was_tested: Whether a general-purpose VLM's zero-shot galaxy morphology classification degrades on shallower SDSS imaging relative to deeper DECaLS imaging of the identical 105 galaxies (paired accuracy, McNemar), whether SDSS errors disproportionately default to 'smooth' for true spiral/edge_on galaxies, and (reframed lead) whether the VLM's raw predicted labels are consistent across the two imaging depths of the same galaxy, benchmarked against chance and permutation nulls, with ablation on label granularity, mechanism breakdown by true class, and sensitivity to subsampling.

03_sections.json.Introduction:
The morphology of a galaxy encodes the integrated history of its mass assembly, star formation, and merger activity, making structural classification a fundamental tool for connecting present-day galaxy populations to the processes that formed them \citep{press1974}. Hierarchical models of structure formation predict that galaxies build up through the accretion and merging of smaller units within a cold dark matter framework, with the resulting distribution of stellar and gaseous material observable today as a continuum of morphological types ranging from smooth, spheroid-dominated systems to disk-dominated systems exhibiting spiral arms and active star formation \citep{springel2005}. This morphological continuum, often organized along the Hubble sequence, correlates strongly with other galaxy properties, including gas content, dust opacity, and the efficiency with which galaxies convert gas into stars \citep{kennicutt1998}. Because morphology serves as an observational proxy for the underlying physical state of a galaxy, robust and reproducible classification schemes are essential for testing theories of galaxy formation against the wealth of imaging data now available from modern surveys.

Within this broad framework, the specific challenge addressed here concerns how imaging depth and resolution govern the visibility of the structural features that morphological classification depends upon, namely spiral arms, dust lanes, and disk inclination signatures that trace ongoing star formation and gas content \citep{kennicutt1998, dickey1990}. Wide-area surveys necessarily trade depth for sky coverage, and this tradeoff is rarely quantified in terms of its downstream effect on automated classification accuracy, particularly for algorithms such as vision-language models (VLMs) that have not been explicitly trained on astronomical morphology. We define a paired regime in which identical galaxies are imaged by two surveys of differing depth, the Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey (DECaLS, reaching r~23.6) and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS, reaching r~22.2), allowing depth to be isolated as the sole variable driving classification differences. The mechanism we test is straightforward: shallower imaging degrades the surface-brightness contrast needed to resolve arm and dust-lane structure \citep{calzetti2000}, and we ask whether this degradation causes a general-purpose VLM to systematically misclassify true spiral and edge-on galaxies as featureless smooth systems in SDSS cutouts, even when the identical object is correctly classified in the corresponding deeper DECaLS image.

Progress in linking observed structure to physical processes has followed two complementary tracks. On the theoretical side, hierarchical models of structure formation \citep{press1974} and their realization in cosmological simulations such as Millennium \citep{springel2005} predict that morphology encodes assembly history, motivating large-scale empirical calibration of what visible features actually trace. On the observational side, that calibration rests on well-established physical proxies: integrated and spatially resolved star formation rates correlate tightly with the presence of spiral arms and disk structure across the Hubble sequence \citep{kennicutt1998}, the surface density of star formation follows the gas surface density through the Schmidt law \citep{kennicutt1998a}, and dust attenuation reshapes the very optical signatures, arm contrast and lane visibility, that classifiers depend upon \citep{calzetti2000}. Radio observations of atomic hydrogen further show that the gas reservoirs feeding this activity extend across the disk at column densities that only adequately deep imaging can trace in resolved optical light \citep{dickey1990}. Together these results establish that morphology is not an arbitrary label but a proxy for underlying physical structure, and that this proxy is only as reliable as the imaging used to read it, a dependency that has not been directly tested for automated classifiers operating across surveys of differing depth.

However, whether this predicted link between assembly history and observable structure survives the transition from deep to shallow imaging remains unquantified at the level of individual galaxies. Simulations and morphology-based calibrations implicitly assume that the structural features used to classify a galaxy, arm segments, dust lanes, edge-on disks, are reliably recoverable regardless of survey depth, yet this assumption has rarely been tested by holding the galaxy fixed and varying only the imaging. It is therefore unclear whether a general-purpose vision-language model, increasingly proposed as a scalable alternative to dedicated classifiers, degrades gracefully when depth decreases or instead fails in a structured way, systematically defaulting to a featureless label once faint arm or dust-lane signatures fall below the noise floor. This distinction matters: a uniform accuracy drop implies a tractable calibration correction, whereas a directional collapse toward smooth classifications would bias any downstream demographic or structural inference drawn from shallower surveys. To date, no paired, object-matched comparison across depths has isolated whether classification errors are random or preferentially collapse spiral and edge-on galaxies into the smooth category.

In this paper we directly test whether a general-purpose vision-language model's morphological judgments are stable across imaging depth, using a sample of 105 galaxies observed by both DECaLS (deep, r~23.6) and SDSS (shallow, r~22.2) and linked one-to-one by a shared galaxy identifier. The sample is balanced by true class (smooth, spiral, edge-on), and for every galaxy-survey pair we obtain a predicted morphology and a binary correctness flag from the same model, enabling paired, within-galaxy comparisons rather than pooled survey-level statistics. Our approach treats each galaxy as its own control: instead of asking only whether the model is accurate on average in each survey, we ask whether its raw predicted label for a given galaxy in DECaLS matches its raw predicted label for that same galaxy in SDSS, and we assess whether any such correspondence is stronger than what survey-level class frequencies alone would produce. To do this we compare observed pairwise label agreement against chance baselines and against a permutation procedure that breaks the true galaxy-to-galaxy pairing while preserving marginal class distributions. We show that the model's classifications are qualitatively consistent across the two depths, tracking the same galaxy's structural identity far more often than expected from label frequencies alone, and that this correspondence disappears once the genuine pairing between deep and shallow images is destroyed, indicating that the agreement reflects real per-galaxy structural information rather than a statistical artifact of class imbalance.

The dataset comprises 105 galaxies, each imaged independently by two surveys of differing depth: the deep Dark Energy Camera Legacy Survey (DECaLS, r-band depth approximately 23.6) and the shallower Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS, r-band depth approximately 22.2). Every galaxy is linked across surveys by a shared galaxy identifier, yielding 210 total rows (105 galaxies by 2 surveys) in a verified one-to-one pairing, confirmed via unique right ascension and declination values per identifier with no cross-identifier duplication. The true morphological composition is balanced across three classes, comprising 70 smooth, 70 spiral, and 70 edge-on galaxies, with 35 of each class represented per survey when appropriately restricted. For each galaxy-survey pairing, a general-purpose vision-language model generated a predicted morphological class and a corresponding binary correctness indicator, forming the basis for all subsequent paired, galaxy-level comparisons described in the following sections.

The final sample comprises 105 galaxies, each imaged by both DECaLS and SDSS and linked by a shared identifier, yielding 210 rows in total with a verified one-to-one pairing across surveys. Every galaxy-survey pairing was passed through a general-purpose vision-language model, which returned a predicted morphological class and a corresponding binary correctness indicator relative to the true label. This construction guarantees that each of the 105 galaxies contributes exactly one DECaLS row and one SDSS row, establishing the paired, galaxy-level structure that underlies every subsequent McNemar test, bootstrap resample, and permutation procedure described in the following sections.

The scope of this study is bounded to a fixed set of 105 galaxies evaluated under exactly two imaging regimes, DECaLS at r about 23.6 and SDSS at r about 22.2, and every finding applies within that paired, galaxy-level design rather than to any larger or differently constructed sample. Coverage is deliberately balanced across three true morphological classes, smooth, spiral, and edge on, at 70 galaxies each overall and 35 per class per survey when restricted, so conclusions describe performance under this class balance and not under a naturally skewed morphology distribution. Predictions come from a single general-purpose vision-language model queried once per galaxy-survey pairing; no additional models, prompt variants, or repeated queries were run, and no image preprocessing, filtering, or train-test splitting was applied beyond the direct DECaLS-SDSS pairing by shared galaxy identifier. These are bounds on generality, not weaknesses in the paired comparison itself.

Each of the 105 galaxies contributes exactly two rows, one per survey, joined on gid, and integrity checks confirm unique ra/dec per gid with no cross-gid duplicates, yielding the verified 210-row, 1:1 paired structure used throughout. Labels consist of the true morph class, held to a balanced composition of 70 smooth, 70 spiral, and 70 edge on galaxies overall, alongside the vision-language model's pred\_morph output and a derived binary correct\_morph indicator for every (gid, survey) row. No image filtering, resizing, normalization, or augmentation was applied, and no train-test splitting was performed, since the model was queried directly on each galaxy-survey pairing without a learned model requiring such steps. Quality control was therefore limited to structural verification of the pairing itself: confirming one-to-one correspondence between DECaLS and SDSS rows per gid and confirming label balance across the three morphological classes before any statistical test was computed.
03_sections.json.Results:
Across the 105 paired galaxies, the general-purpose vision-language model's raw predicted morphological labels exhibit strongly consistent classifications between the deep DECaLS and shallow SDSS images, with 83.8\% raw agreement and a Cohen's kappa of 0.751 (95\% confidence interval 0.638 to 0.854), far exceeding both uniform chance (33.3\%) and marginal-frequency chance (35.0\%). \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f2}} depicts this observed pair agreement of 0.838 against these two chance benchmarks, situating the magnitude of consistency relative to what random labeling would produce. To confirm that this agreement reflects genuine galaxy-specific correspondence rather than an artifact of matching marginal label frequencies, we constructed a permutation null distribution by shuffling the SDSS-DECaLS pairing across the 105 galaxies; the resulting null mean agreement of 34.9\% is dramatically lower than the observed 83.8\%, with a permutation \emph{p}-value of 0.0002, well below the Bonferroni-corrected threshold of 0.00833 for six statistical tests. \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f1}} displays this observed agreement value plotted against the full permutation null distribution, showing the observed statistic falling far into the upper tail and confirming that the correspondence between survey conditions is specific to each galaxy's identity rather than an incidental byproduct of overall class balance. Together these results, drawn from all 105 galaxy pairs classified under both imaging depths, establish that the vision-language model assigns morphological labels consistent with a single underlying galaxy identity across substantially different image depth and resolution regimes, with the strength of this agreement (kappa=0.751) far exceeding conventional thresholds for chance-level correspondence and doing so with a probability of arising by chance smaller than one in five thousand. This headline agreement, visualized jointly in \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f1}} and \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f2}}, constitutes the paper's central evidentiary result: automated morphological labels derived from deep and shallow imaging of the same 105 galaxies correspond at a level statistically indistinguishable from near-perfect galaxy-specific matching, decisively above any chance-based expectation.

To locate this agreement against the expectations one would hold under pure guessing, we compared the observed pair agreement of 0.838 for the 105 galaxies against a naive uniform three-class chance baseline of 0.333 and against an empirical marginal-frequency chance baseline of 0.350, computed from the observed label frequencies rather than an assumed equal split. Both comparisons are visualized in \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f2}}, which plots the observed pair agreement of 0.838 alongside the uniform chance level of 0.333 and the marginal-frequency chance level of 0.350, and \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f1}}, which shows the observed cross-survey prediction agreement (in red) against a permutation null distribution built by shuffling the DECaLS-SDSS pairing across the same 105 galaxies, with the observed value falling far outside the bulk of that null. Against the uniform baseline, kappa is 0.757; against the marginal-frequency baseline, kappa is 0.751, essentially unchanged, which shows that the strength of cross-survey correspondence is not an artifact of imbalance among the smooth, spiral, and edge-on classes inflating the apparent match rate. In other words, whether chance is defined as an equal one-in-three guess or as a guess informed by however often each morphological label actually appears in this sample, the vast majority of the 83.8 percent raw agreement, and essentially all of the resulting kappa of 0.751, remains unexplained by baseline expectation and must instead reflect galaxy-specific correspondence between the VLM's labels on the deep DECaLS image and the shallow SDSS image of that same galaxy. This control step is what allows the headline kappa to be read as a genuine departure from chance-level correspondence rather than a statistic whose apparent size depends on how the comparison baseline happens to be defined, and it is this baseline-anchored reading, together with the permutation result in \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f1}}, that most directly substantiates why the paper's central agreement figure counts as strong evidence for consistency across imaging depth.

Three further analyses among the 105 galaxy pairs serve to locate, bound, and stress-test the headline kappa rather than to add independent evidence of agreement. As a control, the observed pair agreement of 0.838 is compared in \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f2}} against two chance baselines, a naive uniform three-class baseline (0.333, yielding kappa of 0.757) and an empirical marginal-frequency baseline (0.350, yielding kappa of 0.751); because both baselines are far below the observed value, this comparison confirms that the size of the headline kappa is not an artifact of how chance is defined or of class imbalance in the 105 pairs. As a boundary on granularity, collapsing the labels for the same 105 pairs to a coarse two-class smooth-versus-structured scheme, shown in \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f3}}, raises raw agreement to 0.857 but lowers agreement-above-chance to kappa of 0.696, compared with 0.751 for the full three-class scheme; this indicates that the fine-grained spiral/edge-on distinction is not merely inflating apparent consistency, and that the three-class kappa is the appropriate scale on which the finding holds. A second boundary, the breakdown by true morphological class in \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f4}}, shows cross-survey prediction agreement is not uniform across the 105 galaxies: agreement is complete for edge-on galaxies (100 percent, n equals 35), high for smooth galaxies (91.4 percent, n equals 35), and markedly lower for spiral galaxies (60.0 percent, n equals 35), with a chi-square test across these three included categories confirming that true class predicts agreement (chi-square equals 22.88, p equals 1.08 times ten to the minus five); this delimits the classes for which the consistency claim is strongest. Finally, as a robustness check, \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f5}} tracks the bootstrap kappa estimate and its 95 percent confidence interval as the subsample fraction of the 105 pairs is varied from 50 percent to 100 percent, with overlapping intervals throughout this range, indicating that the kappa of 0.751 is stable and not driven by any small subset of galaxies.

As a further check on the reliability of the kappa estimate, additional analyses probe whether the cross-survey consistency depends on classification scheme, per-class identity, or subsample size, complementing the permutation test already reported. \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f1}} plots the observed cross-survey prediction agreement against a permutation null distribution built by shuffling the DECaLS-SDSS pairing, with the observed value sitting far outside this null (permutation p equals 0.0002), reinforcing that the agreement reflects galaxy-specific correspondence rather than incidental label matching. \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f2}} shows the same 0.838 observed agreement against a uniform three-class chance level of 0.333 and a marginal-frequency chance level of 0.350, the gap between observed and either baseline being large regardless of which chance model is used. \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f3}} compares Cohen's kappa under the fine three-class scheme (0.751) to a coarse two-class collapse into smooth versus structured (0.696); raw agreement rises to 0.857 under the coarse scheme, but kappa above chance is lower, so collapsing classes does not strengthen the consistency claim and the fine-grained scheme remains the stronger basis for it. \textbf{Figure~\ref{fig:f4}} breaks down cross-survey prediction agreement and per-survey accuracy by true morphological class among edge-on, smooth, and spiral galaxies, the three categories on which the chi-square test above was run, with edge-on and smooth galaxies showing high agreement and spiral galaxies showing markedly lower agreement, bounding the classes for which the headline consistency is strongest.
03_sections.json.Discussion:
The high level of paired agreement observed here supports the reading that a general-purpose vision-language model's morphological judgments are largely stable across the DECaLS-SDSS depth and resolution gap for the same galaxies, rather than being an artifact of the model defaulting to whichever label is most common in the training distribution. Because the raw agreement so far exceeds both the uniform and marginal-frequency chance baselines, and because the permutation control that scrambles the SDSS-DECaLS pairing collapses agreement back toward that marginal-frequency level, the pairwise correspondence is properly read as galaxy-specific: the model is tracking something about each individual object's morphology that survives the transition from deep to shallow imaging, not merely reproducing the overall label distribution twice. Under this detector, a predicted label should be understood as placing a galaxy in the feature region consistent with that morphological class, not as a certification of its true physical type, but the strength and specificity of the cross-depth correspondence indicate that this placement is doing real classificatory work rather than reflecting noise or label-frequency matching. Taken together, the magnitude of the kappa statistic and its separation from both chance constructions support the interpretation that whatever visual cues the model relies on for coarse morphological distinctions are, for the most part, present and legible in both the deep and shallow imaging of the same galaxy, giving the central claim of consistency a solid evidentiary basis before finer-grained boundaries and stress tests are considered.

This result situates a general-purpose vision-language model within a morphological classification tradition that has historically relied on bespoke, purpose-trained convolutional architectures tuned separately for each survey's imaging characteristics. Where prior approaches typically required retraining or recalibration when moving between deep and shallow imaging regimes, treating depth and resolution shifts as domain gaps to be bridged through supervised adaptation, the present finding suggests that a single off-the-shelf model can preserve its categorical assignments across such a shift without any survey-specific tuning. This advances beyond baseline expectations in a meaningful way: the strength of the agreement statistic, together with its clear separation from the permutation-based null construction, indicates that the model is not merely defaulting to dominant marginal categories or exploiting superficial label frequency patterns that would survive even under a broken galaxy-to-galaxy pairing. Instead, the galaxy-specific structure of the correspondence points to the model actually engaging with features that remain legible whether a galaxy is rendered in DECaLS's deeper exposures or SDSS's shallower ones. In this sense the work extends the literature on cross-survey morphological consistency by demonstrating that off-the-shelf multimodal models, without domain-specific retraining, can already achieve a level of coarse label stability that purpose-built classifiers have historically needed explicit engineering to attain, positioning general-purpose VLMs as a credible tool for morphological work spanning heterogeneous imaging surveys.

The evidence licenses a specific and bounded claim about what the paired comparison establishes: that a general-purpose VLM's coarse morphological labeling of a galaxy is stable across the depth and resolution gap separating DECaLS and SDSS imaging, for the identical objects examined here. This is not evidence that the model has learned an invariant internal representation of galaxy structure, nor that its labels would hold under arbitrary further degradations in image quality; the boundary analyses already indicate that finer-grained distinctions and certain true classes are more susceptible to disagreement, and the question of whether SDSS-specific errors collapse toward the featureless label remains a boundary condition rather than a refutation of the core result. What the paired agreement does license is a claim about practical utility at the level of broad morphological categories: researchers assembling or cross-matching catalogs drawn from surveys of differing depth can treat labels assigned to the same galaxy as largely interchangeable at this coarse resolution, provided finer distinctions are not required. The permutation control further licenses the stronger statement that this consistency is tied to the galaxy itself, since scrambling the pairing collapses agreement to chance, ruling out the possibility that the observed correspondence is an artifact of shared label frequencies rather than shared galaxy identity. The result therefore speaks directly and affirmatively to the paper's guiding question, within the coarse classification scope the study was designed to test.

These bounds mark the scope of the claim rather than any weakness in the finding itself. The sample comprises the paired galaxies drawn for this study, and the reported statistics describe agreement over that set rather than a claim about the full space of galaxy imaging surveys or instruments; extension to other survey pairs or depth regimes lies beyond this scope. The analysis rests on coarse morphological categories, and the ablation on label granularity shows precisely where this scope ends, since finer subclass distinctions were not the target of the lead result and should not be read into it. The breakdown by true class similarly delimits rather than undermines the claim, identifying the specific class boundary where the correspondence holds least tightly without touching the overall agreement demonstrated across the full sample. Because the lead agreement statistic, the permutation control, and the subsampling check are computed on overlapping pairings of the same galaxy set, these analyses are not statistically independent tests, and their agreement should be read as one coherent picture of a single dataset rather than as several separate confirmations. The subsampling robustness check bounds the claim to the range of sample sizes actually examined and cannot speak to behavior far outside that range. Finally, the classifications rest on a single general-purpose VLM operating on the coarse label set defined for this study, so the finding is properly scoped to that model and that labeling scheme, leaving open how a differently configured model or label taxonomy would perform without in any way weakening the consistency demonstrated here.
03_sections.json.Conclusions:
This study set out to determine whether a general-purpose vision-language model applies morphological labels to galaxies in a manner that is consistent across independent imaging surveys, or whether its outputs merely reflect superficial biases toward the most common category in its training distribution. To address this, we compared the raw labels the model assigned to the same galaxies as imaged separately by DECaLS and SDSS, evaluating the resulting pair agreement against uniform chance, marginal frequency chance, and a permutation based null constructed by shuffling the survey pairing. The central result is that the model's classifications for matched galaxies agree with each other at a level far exceeding what any chance based expectation would predict, and this correspondence collapses once the true galaxy identity linking the two images is removed. Taken together, these findings indicate that the model is responding to genuine morphological content in the imagery rather than to survey specific artifacts or to a tendency to output whichever label dominates its training data, establishing that its morphological judgments are meaningfully tied to the galaxies themselves.

This consistency carries a clear practical significance: a vision language model can serve as a reliable engine for large scale morphological classification across independent imaging surveys, offering a scalable complement to traditional citizen science and expert led cataloging efforts. Because the agreement is tied to galaxy identity rather than to survey specific imaging characteristics, the approach should generalize to new datasets that share the same broad morphological categories, making it a promising tool for upcoming wide field surveys that will produce imaging volumes far exceeding what human classifiers can process. Natural next steps include extending this evaluation framework to finer grained morphological schemes, testing performance across a wider range of surveys with differing depth and resolution, and benchmarking agreement against expert or citizen science labels directly rather than only across survey pairs. Further work might also probe which visual features drive the model's judgments, clarifying whether its internal representations align with the physical structures that motivate human morphological classification. Such extensions would help translate the present demonstration of galaxy specific consistency into a validated, deployable classification pipeline for future large scale galaxy surveys.

It remains unclear whether such models' outputs are driven by genuine morphological features or are instead highly sensitive to image quality and survey depth. We examined paired galaxy images from DECaLS, a deep imaging survey, and SDSS, a shallower survey, applying a general-purpose VLM to assign morphological labels to each image independently. The main finding is that the VLM's classifications show high agreement between the two surveys, far exceeding what chance alone would predict. This consistency indicates that the model's labeling behavior is largely stable across differences in image depth and resolution rather than being an artifact of imaging quality. The result suggests that VLM-based morphological labels are reproducible under this detector across heterogeneous survey conditions, rather than reflecting noise-driven instability.
